visuals.title: Where AIHA red cells die
visuals.text: Warm (IgG): splenic macrophages eat coated cells, making spherocytes. Cold (IgM): complement lyses cells inside vessels.

visuals.title: Why aplasia hits every line
visuals.text: All three fall together: pancytopenia, not isolated anaemia.

glossary.Haemoglobin: The iron-containing protein in red cells that carries oxygen.
glossary.Hb: Haemoglobin, measured in g/L on a full blood count.
glossary.Oxygen-carrying capacity: How much oxygen the blood can carry, set mainly by haemoglobin level.
glossary.Malabsorption: Poor absorption of nutrients from the gut, for example in coeliac disease.
glossary.Pallor: Unusual paleness of the skin or inner eyelids.
glossary.Conjunctival pallor: Pale lining of the lower eyelid, a bedside sign of anaemia.
glossary.Palpitations: An unpleasant awareness of your own heartbeat.
glossary.Tachycardia: A heart rate over 100 beats per minute.
glossary.Developmental delay: A child reaching milestones such as walking or talking later than expected.
glossary.Serum iron: The amount of iron circulating in the blood, bound to transferrin.
glossary.CKD: Chronic kidney disease; less erythropoietin is made, causing normocytic anaemia.
glossary.B12: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin), needed for DNA synthesis in red cell precursors and for healthy nerves.
glossary.Folate: A B vitamin needed for DNA synthesis; deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia.
glossary.Jaundice: Yellowing of skin and eyes from raised bilirubin.
glossary.Prosthetic heart valve: An artificial heart valve; mechanical ones can shear red cells.
glossary.Lymphoproliferative malignancy: A cancer of lymphocytes, such as CLL or lymphoma.
glossary.Autoantibodies: Antibodies that attack the body's own tissues.
glossary.IgG: The main antibody class in the blood; it causes warm AIHA.
glossary.IgM: A large antibody class that fixes complement well; it causes cold AIHA.
glossary.Ciprofloxacin: A quinolone antibiotic that can trigger haemolysis.
glossary.Cephalosporin: A class of beta-lactam antibiotics, such as ceftriaxone.
glossary.Methyldopa: An older blood pressure drug, used in pregnancy, that can cause warm AIHA.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen.
glossary.Parietal cells: Stomach cells that make acid and intrinsic factor.
glossary.Terminal ileum: The last part of the small intestine, where B12 is absorbed.
glossary.Peripheral neuropathy: Damage to nerves in the limbs, causing numbness, tingling or weakness.
glossary.Hashimoto's disease: Autoimmune thyroiditis, the commonest cause of hypothyroidism.
glossary.Type 1 diabetes: Autoimmune destruction of insulin-making pancreatic cells.
glossary.X-linked recessive: Inherited on the X chromosome; mostly affects males, females are usually carriers.
glossary.Oxidative stress: Damage from reactive oxygen chemicals that outstrips the cell's antioxidant defences.
glossary.Fava beans: Broad beans; they contain oxidants that trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Nitrofurantoin: An antibiotic for urinary infections; an oxidant trigger in G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Primaquine: An antimalarial drug that can trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Sulphonylureas: Diabetes tablets such as gliclazide; sulpha-type drugs that can trigger G6PD haemolysis.
glossary.Sulpha-drugs: Sulphonamide-containing drugs such as co-trimoxazole; oxidant triggers in G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Megaloblastic: Large, immature red cell precursors from faulty DNA synthesis, as in B12 or folate deficiency.
glossary.Non-megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia: Large red cells without megaloblasts, for example from hypothyroidism, alcohol or liver disease.
glossary.Hypothyroidism: An underactive thyroid with too little thyroid hormone.
glossary.Proximal myopathy: Weakness of the muscles near the trunk, such as the hips and shoulders.
glossary.Fibrin: The protein mesh that forms the framework of a blood clot.
glossary.Focal neurology: Neurological signs affecting one area, such as weakness of one limb.
glossary.Haematopoietic stem cells: Bone marrow stem cells that make all blood cell types.
glossary.Slapped cheek: Bright red cheek rash of parvovirus B19 infection (fifth disease).
glossary.SLE: Systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease affecting many organs.
glossary.Erythropoiesis: Production of red blood cells in the bone marrow.
glossary.Ineffective erythropoiesis: Red cell precursors are made but die in the marrow before maturing.
glossary.Lead poisoning: Toxicity from lead exposure; it blocks haem synthesis and can cause sideroblastic anaemia.
glossary.Isoniazid: A tuberculosis drug that depletes pyridoxine and can cause sideroblastic anaemia.
glossary.Pyridoxine: Vitamin B6, needed for the first step of haem synthesis.
glossary.Autosomal dominant: Inherited so one faulty copy of a gene is enough to cause disease.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a sudden fall in kidney function.
glossary.Creatinine: A muscle waste product cleared by the kidneys; a rise shows falling kidney function.
glossary.Pentad: A group of five classic features.
glossary.Triad: A group of three classic features.
glossary.Bone marrow aspiration: Sucking a liquid marrow sample through a needle, usually from the hip bone, to look at cells.
glossary.Bone marrow biopsy: Taking a core of marrow tissue to see its structure and cellularity.
glossary.Colorectal cancer: Cancer of the colon or rectum; can bleed slowly and cause iron deficiency.
glossary.Suspected cancer pathway: An urgent NHS referral route to be seen within two weeks.
glossary.Bulk-forming laxatives: Fibre laxatives such as ispaghula that soften stool by holding water.
glossary.IV iron: Iron given into a vein, which raises iron stores faster than tablets.
glossary.Prednisolone: An oral corticosteroid that suppresses the immune system.
glossary.Immunosuppressives: Drugs that dampen the immune system, such as azathioprine.
glossary.Haemodynamic instability: Low blood pressure, fast pulse or poor perfusion showing the circulation is failing.
glossary.Blood transfusion: Giving donated red cells into a vein.
glossary.Haem: The iron-containing ring in haemoglobin that binds oxygen.
glossary.Haem synthesis: The chain of reactions that builds haem; it needs iron.
glossary.Erythroid precursors: Immature cells in the marrow that develop into red cells.
glossary.Haemoglobinisation: Filling a developing red cell with haemoglobin.
glossary.Extravascular haemolysis: Red cell destruction outside blood vessels, mainly by spleen and liver macrophages.
glossary.Intravascular haemolysis: Red cells bursting inside blood vessels, releasing haemoglobin into the plasma.
glossary.Complement: A group of blood proteins that can punch holes in coated cells.
glossary.Macrophages: Large immune cells that engulf and digest cells and debris.
glossary.Denatured haemoglobin: Haemoglobin damaged by oxidation so it clumps together.
glossary.Pluripotent: Able to become many different cell types.
